chapter_summary:
Now that you can confidently move around your 3D scene, it's time to learn how to interact with the objects within it. The ability to select and manipulate objects is fundamental to all 3D modeling tasks. Without it, your beautiful navigation skills would be pointless! In Blender, objects are the building blocks of your scene, whether they are meshes, cameras, lights, or even empty containers.

Let's start with **selection**. By default, Blender uses **Left-click** to select objects. If you're coming from other 3D software, you might be used to right-click selection, but don't worry, Blender's preferences allow you to change this if you wish (`Edit > Preferences > Keymap > Select With`). To select a single object, simply click on it. You'll notice a bright orange outline appearing around the selected object, indicating it's active. To deselect an object, click anywhere in an empty space in the 3D Viewport, or press `Alt+A`.

Selecting multiple objects is just as important. You can extend your selection by holding down **Shift** and clicking on additional objects. Each object you click while holding Shift will be added to your current selection. To select all objects in the scene, press **A**. To deselect all, press `Alt+A` (or `A` twice quickly). For more advanced selection, Blender offers **Box Select** (drag with Left-click in empty space), **Circle Select** (press `C` and paint over objects), and **Lasso Select** (Ctrl + Left-click drag). These tools are incredibly powerful for quickly isolating specific groups of objects, especially in complex scenes with many assets. For game development, you might use box select to quickly grab all environmental props in a specific area of your level, or select multiple parts of a modular character.

Next, let's talk about the **3D Cursor**. This often-misunderstood element is a red and white crosshair that you'll see in your scene. By default, it starts at the world origin (0,0,0). The 3D Cursor serves several crucial purposes: it dictates where new objects are created, and it can act as a pivot point for transformations. You can move the 3D Cursor by **Shift + Right-click** anywhere in the 3D Viewport. To snap it back to the world origin, press `Shift+S` and choose "Cursor to World Origin." Understanding the 3D Cursor is key to precise placement and manipulation, ensuring your new objects appear exactly where you intend them to be.

Once an object is selected, you can transform it. **Transformations** refer to changing an object's position (Move), orientation (Rotate), or size (Scale). Blender provides dedicated **transformation gizmos** for each of these operations, located in the toolbar on the left side of the 3D Viewport (or accessible via hotkeys).

*   **Move (Grab) Tool:** Select the "Move" tool (the four-headed arrow icon) or press **G** (for Grab). A gizmo with X, Y, and Z axes will appear on your selected object. You can click and drag on these colored arrows to move the object along a specific axis, or click and drag the white circle in the center to move it freely on the active view plane. Moving objects precisely is critical for level design in games, ensuring assets align perfectly within the game world grid.
    *   **Common Mistake:** Accidentally moving an object off-axis, leading to misalignment. To constrain movement to a single axis after pressing `G`, press `X`, `Y`, or `Z` immediately. For example, `G` then `X` will only move the object along the X-axis. You can also press `Shift+X` to move on all axes *except* X.
*   **Rotate Tool:** Select the "Rotate" tool (the curved arrow icon) or press **R**. A series of colored circles will appear around your object. Dragging on these circles rotates the object around the corresponding axis. The outermost white circle rotates the object relative to your current view.
    *   **Common Mistake:** Rotating an object without considering its origin point (which we'll discuss next). This can lead to unexpected rotations, where the object spins around a distant point rather than its own center.
*   **Scale Tool:** Select the "Scale" tool (the box with arrows icon) or press **S**. A gizmo with colored cubes will appear. Dragging on these cubes scales the object along a specific axis, while dragging the white circle in the center scales it uniformly.
    *   **Common Mistake:** Non-uniform scaling (scaling only on one axis) without intending to, which can distort models and cause issues with UV mapping or physics in a game engine. If you need to scale uniformly, make sure to drag the white circle or press `S` then `Shift+X` (or Y or Z) to scale uniformly on all axes *except* the chosen one.

Each object has an **origin point**, represented by a small orange dot. This point is the pivot around which all transformations (move, rotate, scale) occur. By default, when you create a new object, its origin is at its geometric center. However, you can change an object's origin. For example, if you're modeling a door for a game, you'd want its origin to be at its hinge, so it rotates correctly. To change the origin, select your object, go to `Object > Set Origin`, and choose an option like "Origin to 3D Cursor" or "Origin to Geometry." Understanding and correctly setting the origin is a critical skill for creating functional game assets like animated props or characters.

Finally, **snapping** is a powerful feature for precise placement. You can enable snapping by clicking the magnet icon in the header of the 3D Viewport, or by holding **Ctrl** during a transformation. Blender can snap to various elements like increment (grid), vertex, edge, face, and volume. For instance, when building modular game environments, snapping to vertices or edges ensures that different pieces of your environment (like walls or floor tiles) connect seamlessly without gaps. This precision is invaluable for maintaining a clean and functional game world, reducing errors and saving time.

screens.title: Selecting and Manipulating Objects
screens.subtitle: How to pick, move, rotate, scale, and place objects precisely in Blender

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn the core interactions that let you shape a scene: selecting objects, positioning the 3D Cursor, transforming objects with Move, Rotate and Scale, setting an object's origin, and snapping for precise alignment. These are the building blocks for every modeling task — from arranging simple props to preparing assets for a game engine. You will see concrete examples like isolating multiple props, moving a cube along a single axis, and setting a door's origin to its hinge so rotations behave correctly. We'll also clear up common confusions: why your object might rotate around a distant point, and how snapping differs from grid increments or vertex-to-vertex alignment. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to select single or multiple objects with confidence, choose the right transformation tool or hotkey, and use the 3D Cursor and origin settings to control pivot behavior. Keep an eye out for the hands-on steps where you'll transform the default cube and test snapping and origin changes yourself. Ready to begin and make each interaction deliberate and precise?

keyIdea.text: Selecting and transforming objects is the foundation of modeling workflows; mastering these controls saves time and prevents alignment and animation errors.

narration.text: These four objectives map directly to the hands-on skills you need. First, you will master techniques for selecting single and multiple objects so you can isolate and organize parts of a scene. For example, using Shift-click and box selection lets you gather assets quickly when blocking a game level. Second, you'll understand the 3D Cursor: where it sits, how to move it, and how it controls where new objects appear and can act as a pivot. Third, you'll confidently use Move, Rotate, and Scale using both gizmos and the G, R, and S hotkeys, including axis constraints like G then X. That skill prevents unintentional distortions. Fourth, you'll explain and set an object's origin point and use snapping to position objects precisely. Knowing when to set origin to geometry or to cursor is key for predictable rotations. Each objective is paired with a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check your progress as you practice in the lab.

screens.title: Selection Basics
screens.subtitle: Left-click selection, orange outline, and deselection shortcuts

narration.text: Selection is how you tell Blender which object or objects you intend to work on. The default method is Left-click: when you click an object it becomes selected and will show a bright orange outline indicating it is active. Deselecting is equally important: clicking empty space or pressing Alt+A clears your current selection so you can start a new one. If you come from other software with right-click selection, Blender lets you change that preference, but it's best to learn the default left-click behavior first because many tutorials and shortcuts assume it. A common misstep is assuming selection is persistent across modes; selections persist within Object Mode, but edit-mode vertex selections are a different context. A concrete example: when you import a character and want to move only the hat, left-click the hat and confirm the orange outline before transforming. Misconception to avoid: the orange outline does not indicate a child or parent relationship — it simply marks the active object. Key takeaway: always verify the orange indicator and use Alt+A when you need a clean slate before selecting a new set of objects.

keyIdea.title: Selection rule
keyIdea.text: Left-click selects; orange outline marks active object; Alt+A deselects — confirm before transforming.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Selection Basics
Definition

Selecting objects with Left-click

Selection marks which object will receive edits. The orange outline shows the active selection and ensures transformations apply to the intended target.

Quick checks
  • Left-click to select. Orange outline appears.
  • Click empty space or press Alt+A to deselect all.
  • Use Preferences if you prefer right-click selection.
Common Mistake

Confusing selection contexts: selecting in Object Mode differs from Edit Mode vertex selections. Confirm the mode before editing.

Example Scenario

You imported a character and want to move only a hat. Left-click the hat, confirm the orange outline, then use Move. If the outline is missing, transformations will affect the wrong object.

Key Takeaway

Always confirm selection visually before performing transforms to avoid accidental edits.

Check Your Understanding

If a transform moves unexpected geometry, what two checks should you make before continuing?

screens.title: Selecting Multiple Objects
screens.subtitle: Shift-click, A/all, Box, Circle, and Lasso Select techniques

narration.text: Selecting multiple objects gives you the ability to edit several assets as a group, which is essential for layout and batch transforms. The simplest method is to hold Shift and click additional objects; each object clicked is added to the selection. Press A to select all objects in the scene and Alt+A to deselect everything. For visual selection tools, Box Select lets you drag a rectangle to include objects inside it, Circle Select (press C) lets you paint over objects to select them, and Lasso Select (Ctrl+Left-drag) traces a freeform area. A real example: when assembling a modular room, use Box Select to grab all furniture inside a single room and then G to move them together. A common misconception is that these tools always pick visible geometry — they select object origins. If objects overlap visually, toggle selection visibility or orbit the view to ensure correct picks. Key takeaway: combine Shift-click with boxed or painted tools for fast, accurate multi-selection in complex scenes. Selecting Multiple Objects means shift-click for additive selection, a for all, and box/circle/lasso tools for quick group selection in dense scenes.. In practical terms, shift-click, a/all, box, circle, and lasso select techniques. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multi-select workflow
keyIdea.text: Shift-click for additive selection, A for all, and box/circle/lasso tools for quick group selection in dense scenes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Selecting Multiple Objects
Selection Tools

Add, All, and Visual Selection

  • Shift + Left-click: Add objects to selection one by one.
  • A: Select all. Alt + A: Deselect all.
  • Box Select: Drag to select by rectangle; Circle Select (C): paint select; Lasso: freehand region.
Misconception

These tools select object origins, not visible pixels; overlapping objects can hide origins. Orbit the view if selection seems wrong.

Example

To move all props in a room, use Box Select to capture them, then press G to move the group while maintaining layout relationships.

Key Takeaway

Combine additive clicks with region tools to select exactly the objects you need in complex scenes.

Try this

Use Circle Select to quickly collect scattered props, then deselect any extras with Shift-click.

screens.title: The 3D Cursor Explained
screens.subtitle: Where new objects appear and how it can act as a pivot

narration.text: The 3D Cursor is a simple but powerful crosshair that controls two important behaviors: where new objects are created, and where some transformations can pivot from if you choose it as the origin. By default it sits at the world origin, but you can move it quickly with Shift+Right-click anywhere in the 3D Viewport. Use Shift+S to open the snap menu and choose 'Cursor to World Origin' when you need to reset it. A common practical use is precise placement: move the cursor to a corner, then add a new object and it will appear exactly at that cursor location, saving you from manual repositioning. Another workflow is to set an object's origin to the cursor, enabling rotations around that cursor point; for example, place the cursor at a hinge location and set Origin to 3D Cursor so a door rotates correctly. Misconception check: the cursor is not a selection tool — it does not make objects active by itself. Key takeaway: learn to place and reset the cursor often; it gives you deterministic control over object placement and pivoting.

keyIdea.title: Cursor power
keyIdea.text: The 3D Cursor sets creation position and can become a pivot when combined with origin settings, enabling precise placement and predictable rotations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › 3D Cursor Explained
What is the 3D Cursor?

Placement and pivot control

Move the cursor with Shift+Right-click. Reset with Shift+S → Cursor to World Origin. New objects appear at the cursor and you can set an origin to the cursor for pivoted transforms.

Practical Use

Place the cursor at a hinge point, set origin to cursor, then rotate the object to behave like a real hinge.

Example

To create a lamp at a precise spot, move the cursor to that spot and add the lamp; it appears exactly where you placed the cursor.

Key Takeaway

Use the cursor to control where things are created and to define non-standard pivots for predictable transforms.

Common Mistake

Assuming the cursor selects objects. It only sets positions and potential pivot points.

screens.title: Move (Grab) Tool & Axis Constraints
screens.subtitle: Using the Move gizmo, G hotkey, and constraining to X/Y/Z

narration.text: Moving objects precisely is central to layout and alignment. Use the Move tool's gizmo to drag along colored arrows or grab the center for free movement on the view plane. The hotkey G activates Grab quickly; after pressing G, press X, Y, or Z to constrain movement to that axis. For instance, pressing G then X will let you slide an asset along the X-axis only. If you want to move on all axes except one, press Shift plus the axis — for example G then Shift+X moves on Y and Z while restricting X. These constraints help avoid accidental off-axis shifts that break alignment in a modular level. A typical workflow: select a prop, press G then Z to raise it along height, and Left-click to confirm. Misconception check: the gizmo arrow direction follows object orientation when in local transform mode; confirm transform orientation if you need global axis movement. Key takeaway: combine the gizmo for visual control with G plus immediate axis keys for fast, precise moves. Move (Grab) Tool & Axis Constraints means use g for quick grabs and press x, y, or z immediately to lock movement to a single axis; use shift+axis to exclude an axis when needed.. In practical terms, using the move gizmo, g hotkey, and constraining to x/y/z. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Move with precision
keyIdea.text: Use G for quick grabs and press X, Y, or Z immediately to lock movement to a single axis; use Shift+axis to exclude an axis when needed.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Move Tool & Axis Constraints
Move Tool

Gizmos and hotkeys for controlled translation

  • Activate Move with the four-headed arrow gizmo or press G.
  • After G, press X, Y, or Z to constrain to that axis. Press Shift+Axis to exclude an axis.
  • Use gizmo arrows for visual control; the center circle moves on the view plane.
Misconception

If your object moves along unexpected directions, check whether Transform Orientation is Local vs Global; local axes follow object rotation.

Example

To slide a floor tile into place without raising it, press G then X or Y to constrain movement and avoid changing height accidentally.

Key Takeaway

Use axis constraints immediately after pressing G to move accurately and prevent misaligned placements.

Pro Tip

When precision matters, type numeric offsets after constraining to an axis to move by exact amounts.

screens.title: Rotate Tool and Pivot Behavior
screens.subtitle: R hotkey, gizmo circles, view-axis rotation, and origin effects

narration.text: Rotation changes an object's orientation and is performed with the Rotate tool or the R hotkey. When you activate Rotate, you see colored circles that represent rotation around the X, Y, and Z axes. Dragging a circle rotates the object around that axis; using the outer white circle rotates relative to your view. A crucial concept is the object's origin point: rotation always happens around the origin. If an origin is far from the geometry, the object will swing around that distant point, which often surprises beginners. A concrete example is a door: if its origin is at the center, it will spin oddly; set the origin to the hinge and rotations behave like a real door. A common mistake is rotating before checking the origin — if rotation looks wrong, reset or move the origin to the 3D Cursor or to geometry. Key takeaway: always verify or set the origin when planning rotations so your transform behaves predictably. Rotate Tool and Pivot Behavior means rotation occurs around the origin; set the origin to the intended pivot (for example a hinge) to get expected rotation behavior.. In practical terms, r hotkey, gizmo circles, view-axis rotation, and origin effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rotation pivot
keyIdea.text: Rotation occurs around the origin; set the origin to the intended pivot (for example a hinge) to get expected rotation behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Rotate Tool & Pivot Behavior
Rotate Mechanics

R hotkey and gizmo circles

  • Press R to rotate. Use colored circles to rotate around specific axes.
  • The outer white circle rotates relative to the view plane for intuitive adjustments.
  • Rotation always occurs around the object's origin; set it deliberately for correct behavior.
Common Mistake

Rotating before adjusting the origin leads to unexpected motion. If rotation looks wrong, check the origin position first.

Example

For a hinged door, move the 3D Cursor to the hinge, set origin to cursor, then press R and rotate about the correct pivot so the door swings naturally.

Key Takeaway

Set the origin before rotating to make the motion predictable and suited to the object's function.

Check

If rotation seems strange, ask: where is the origin located relative to the geometry?

screens.title: Scale Tool & Uniform vs Axis Scaling
screens.subtitle: S hotkey, gizmo cubes, and avoiding unwanted distortions

narration.text: Scaling changes an object's size and can be performed uniformly or on individual axes. Press S to scale uniformly, dragging to enlarge or shrink while preserving proportions. To scale only on one axis, press S then X, Y, or Z to apply the change to that axis alone. The gizmo shows small cubes for axis-specific scaling and a central white circle for uniform scaling. A common pitfall is accidental non-uniform scaling that distorts models and introduces problems for UVs or physics. For example, a character scaled non-uniformly can create stretched textures and broken animation behavior when exported. If you need to scale uniformly but avoid one axis, use S then Shift+Axis to exclude that axis. Key takeaway: use the uniform handle for proportionate scaling; confirm axis constraints before confirming a transform to prevent downstream model and export issues. Scale Tool & Uniform vs Axis Scaling means prefer uniform scaling for clean topology; use axis constraints intentionally and avoid accidental non-uniform scales that break textures or physics.. In practical terms, s hotkey, gizmo cubes, and avoiding unwanted distortions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scale safely
keyIdea.text: Prefer uniform scaling for clean topology; use axis constraints intentionally and avoid accidental non-uniform scales that break textures or physics.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scale Tool
Scaling Modes

Uniform and axis-specific scaling

  • Press S to scale uniformly. Drag to resize proportionally.
  • Press S then X/Y/Z to restrict scaling to an axis. Use Shift+Axis to exclude an axis.
  • Gizmo cubes indicate axis handles; the center circle is uniform scale.
Common Mistake

Non-uniform scaling can distort UVs and create issues in game physics. Reset scale or apply transforms when needed before export.

Example

Scale a crate uniformly with S to keep textures consistent. If you stretch only X, the wood grain will look distorted and may tile oddly in a game engine.

Key Takeaway

Prefer uniform scaling for assets; use axis scaling only when you intend to alter proportions for design reasons.

Pro Tip

If you must non-uniform scale, consider applying scale transforms before exporting so downstream tools receive uniform transforms.

screens.title: Origin Point and Its Effects
screens.subtitle: What the origin is, default placement, and how to change it

narration.text: An object's origin is a tiny marker that serves as the pivot for all transformations. By default, a newly created object has its origin at its geometric center, but you can change it to the 3D Cursor or to the geometry with Object > Set Origin. Why this matters: rotation and scaling occur around the origin. For instance, if you model a door and want it to rotate at the hinge, place the 3D Cursor at the hinge and set Origin to 3D Cursor so rotations behave as expected. Another example: changing origin to geometry recenters pivot to the visible mesh which is helpful after modifying topology. A common misconception is thinking the origin moves the geometry — the origin is a pivot marker; setting origin to a point does not move the mesh unless you choose 'Origin to Geometry' which recenters the pivot relative to the mesh bounds. Key takeaway: intentionally set origins to control transform behavior and avoid surprises when rotating or scaling assets for animation or export. Origin Point and Its Effects means set an object's origin deliberately to control where rotations and scales occur, matching the object's intended function, like door hinges.. In practical terms, what the origin is, default placement, and how to change it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Origin controls pivot
keyIdea.text: Set an object's origin deliberately to control where rotations and scales occur, matching the object's intended function, like door hinges.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Origin Point & Effects
What is the Origin?

Pivot that controls transforms

The origin is a pivot point. Use Object > Set Origin to move it to the 3D Cursor or to the geometry. It determines where rotations and scales occur.

Usage

Place the origin to match functional parts of the model, such as hinges or attachment points, for correct behavior in animation or game logic.

Example

After moving a lamp model away from origin, use Object > Set Origin > Origin to Geometry to center the pivot at the lamp's visual center for symmetric rotations.

Key Takeaway

The origin does not move geometry by itself; it controls the center for transforms. Set it intentionally for predictable results.

Try this

Move the 3D Cursor to a hinge point, then set Origin to 3D Cursor and rotate to confirm hinge behavior.

screens.title: Snapping Techniques
screens.subtitle: Magnet icon, Increment (grid), Vertex, Edge, Face and Ctrl temporary snap

narration.text: Snapping helps you align objects precisely to other elements in the scene. Enable snapping with the magnet icon in the 3D Viewport header or hold Ctrl during a transformation to temporarily enable snapping. Blender supports several snap types: Increment snaps to the grid for consistent spacing; Vertex snaps align to other object vertices for perfect joins; Edge and Face snapping align to edges or faces, useful when placing objects flush to a surface; Volume snapping can position an object relative to volumes. A practical example is aligning modular wall pieces: choose Vertex snapping to connect corners exactly and avoid gaps. Common mistakes include leaving snapping enabled unintentionally and then wondering why transforms jump; always check the magnet and snap type when transforms behave oddly. Key takeaway: use the magnet for persistent snapping or Ctrl for temporary snaps, and select the snap target that matches the alignment needed — grid for spacing, vertex for joins. Snapping Techniques means enable the magnet for persistent snapping or hold ctrl for a temporary snap; pick increment for grid spacing and vertex to join corners exactly.. In practical terms, magnet icon, increment (grid), vertex, edge, face and ctrl temporary snap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Snap to fit
keyIdea.text: Enable the magnet for persistent snapping or hold Ctrl for a temporary snap; pick Increment for grid spacing and Vertex to join corners exactly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Snapping Techniques
Snap Types

Pick the right snap for the job

  • Increment: snap to grid steps for consistent spacing.
  • Vertex: align to vertices for exact joins.
  • Edge / Face: place objects flush against surfaces.
Workflow Note

Turn snapping on when you need it, and use Ctrl during a transform for a one-off snap without changing the persistent state.

Example

When connecting modular walls, enable Vertex snapping so corners lock together precisely, preventing gaps that can break collision in a game engine.

Key Takeaway

Choose the snap target that matches the alignment task and toggle snapping deliberately to avoid unexpected jumps.

Check

If objects jump while transforming, verify whether snapping is on and which snap type is selected.

screens.title: Transform the Default Cube — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Guided lab: select, move, rotate, scale, change origin, and snap

narration.text: This guided activity walks through the default Cube so you can practice each interaction. First, ensure the Cube is selected; you should see an orange outline. If not, Left-click it. Next, press G to grab the cube and move it freely; Left-click to confirm. Practice axis constraints: press G then X and move the mouse to slide the cube only along X, then confirm. Repeat G then Y and G then Z to experience each axis. For rotation, press R to rotate freely, then R then Z to rotate around Z only; confirm each time. For scaling, press S to scale uniformly, and then try S then Y to change only the Y dimension. Now move the 3D Cursor with Shift+Right-click away from the cube. With the cube selected, choose Object > Set Origin > Origin to 3D Cursor and notice the small orange origin dot move. Press R and rotate to see the cube pivot around the new point. Finally, enable the magnet icon and set snapping to Increment. Press G and watch the cube snap to grid steps; then switch to Vertex snap and try snapping the cube corner to another object's vertex. This sequence demonstrates selection through snapping and highlights how each control affects object behavior.

keyIdea.title: Lab sequence
keyIdea.text: Follow select → move with axis constraints → rotate → scale → set origin → enable snapping to practice predictable transformations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Transform the Default Cube
Step-by-step Lab
  1. Select the default Cube; confirm the orange outline.
  2. Press G to move freely; Left-click to confirm the new location.
  3. Press G then X/Y/Z to constrain movement to a single axis.
  4. Press R to rotate; use R then Z/X/Y for axis-specific rotation.
  5. Press S to scale uniformly; press S then an axis to scale on one axis.
  6. Move the 3D Cursor with Shift+Right-click and use Object > Set Origin > Origin to 3D Cursor.
  7. Enable the magnet and test Increment and Vertex snapping while moving the cube.
Key Takeaway

Practice each step until the behaviors are predictable: selection, axis constraints, origin effects, and snapping.

Example Walkthrough

G then X moves only along X. R then Z rotates around the Z axis. S then Y scales on Y. Set origin to cursor to change pivot for rotation tests.

Checkpoint

After each change, press Alt+A to deselect and reselect the Cube to confirm the transform stuck as expected.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Pro Tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid misaligned transforms and keep a predictable workflow

narration.text: As you build scenes, several recurring mistakes slow beginners down. First, accidental transforms happen when you forget which object is selected or leave snapping on. Always check the orange outline and the magnet state before transforming. Second, rotating with the wrong origin creates unexpected motion; confirm origin location or set it to the 3D Cursor when you need a custom pivot. Third, non-uniform scaling can break textures and animation exports; prefer uniform scaling and apply transforms when necessary before export. Pro tips to avoid these errors: use Alt+A to clear selections before picking the intended objects, toggle snapping only when you need it, and name or isolate objects you plan to edit to reduce accidental picks. A productivity habit is to use the 3D Cursor and set origin workflows when assembling modular assets — placing the cursor at a known anchor reduces guesswork. Final takeaway: build small, repeatable checks into your process so selection, origin, and snapping are deliberate rather than accidental. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Common Mistakes & Pro Tips
Avoid predictable errors

Simple checks and habits keep transforms reliable and assets ready for animation or export.

Mistake: Wrong selection

Confirm the orange outline and consider renaming or isolating the active object to prevent accidental edits.

Mistake: Wrong pivot

Check the origin before rotating. If rotation looks odd, set origin to geometry or cursor as needed.

Mistake: Unintended snapping

Verify the magnet icon when transforms jump unexpectedly. Use Ctrl for temporary snaps instead of leaving snapping on.

Pro Tips
  • Use Alt+A to clear selection before picking a new object.
  • Place the 3D Cursor at precise anchors and set origins for repeated pivot behavior.
  • Apply transforms where necessary before exporting to keep asset behavior consistent.

screens.title: Hotkeys & Practice Checklist
screens.subtitle: Essential hotkeys and a short checklist to rehearse daily

narration.text: A short cheat sheet helps you build fluency. Memorize these keys: G for Grab/Move, R for Rotate, S for Scale, A to select all, Alt+A to deselect, Shift+Right-click to move the 3D Cursor, and Shift+S to snap the cursor to world origin. Box Select and Circle Select give quick region picks and Lasso Select traces freeform areas for complex groups. Use Ctrl during transforms to temporarily enable snapping, or click the magnet icon for persistent snapping. Practice checklist: one, select the default cube and confirm the orange outline; two, move it with G then X, Y, Z; three, rotate with R then Z; four, scale uniformly and on a single axis; five, move the 3D Cursor and set origin to it; six, enable snapping and test both Increment and Vertex modes. Repeat this sequence until each step is predictable. A misconception to avoid is relying on muscle memory without visually confirming the selection and mode; always scan the viewport before confirming a transform. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Short definitions to keep top of mind

narration.text: These three core concepts summarize the chapter and give you mental anchors. Selection means choosing one or more objects to edit; verify the orange outline before transforming. The 3D Cursor is the placement crosshair that determines where new objects appear and can serve as a pivot when you set an origin to it. Transformations — Move, Rotate, Scale — change position, orientation, and size; use gizmos or hotkeys and constrain to axes for precision. Keep these definitions in mind as quick checks while modeling: confirm selection, place the cursor where you want new objects, and choose the right transform and pivot. Practicing these concepts in short cycles builds reliable, repeatable workflows for modeling and game asset creation. narration.text: Keep these concise reminders nearby as you work. First, verify selection visually: the orange outline is your confirmation that transforms will apply to the intended object. Second, the 3D Cursor controls where new objects appear and can be used to position origins for specialized pivots. Third, snapping and axis constraints are your precision tools — use them to avoid gaps and misalignment. These short concepts form a quick checklist you can run mentally before each transform: confirm selection, know the pivot, and set snapping or constraints as needed.
